Summary: The paper introduces a vision–language alignment model, RadZero, for radiology, demonstrating strong zero-shot performance across classification, grounding, and segmentation tasks. There are three main components that contribute to the strong performance of the model: (i) VL-CABS, which computes image–text similarity at the patch level to improve interpretability, (ii) multi-positive contrastive training, enabling effective representation learning without pixel-level annotations, and (iii) support for high-resolution inputs.

Strengths highlighted by the reviewers include:
(i) Transparent and fine-grained visual reasoning that substantially improves clinical interpretability compared to traditional attention maps.
(ii) Comprehensive ablation studies.
(iii) Cohesive integration of multiple ideas into a unified medical VLM.
(iv) Novel and elegant use of cosine similarity as both logit and heatmap in VL-CABS.
(v) Evaluation across nearly all major public chest X-ray datasets, covering a wide range of zero-shot tasks (classification, grounding, segmentation, phrase grounding), which makes the empirical claims convincing.
(vi) High quality of writing, reproducibility, and transparency.
(vii) Clear motivation and logical positioning compared to prior works.
(viii) Intriguing zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation results, where the model can segment anatomical regions in addition to pathology classification.

Weaknesses discussed after rebuttal and discussions include:
(i)  Novelty concerns – raised by Reviewer etwN. Multi-positive contrastive learning has been explored previously, while the application to radiology is novel. The paper does not propose a fundamentally new algorithm.
(ii) Frozen encoder limitation – using encoders at resolutions different from those they were trained on remains an inherent, unresolved technical weakness of the method.

Review process summary and Reasons for decision:  The paper received a mix of borderline reject, borderline accept, accept, and strong accept ratings. The borderline reject primarily stems from the lack of fundamentally new algorithmic contributions. However, taking into account the rebuttal, the feedback from other reviewers, and the strong experimental validation, the AC judges that the paper’s strengths — including its empirical contributions to medical VLMs — outweigh the weaknesses. The recommendation is to accept the paper as a poster.

Additional remarks from the Area Chair and expected changes in the final draft:
(i) The AC notes that the proposed idea is generic and not inherently specific to medical imaging. Therefore, the method should ideally have been evaluated on natural image datasets to demonstrate broader applicability. Alternatively, if the method is tailored specifically for X-ray imaging, the authors should clearly highlight the unique challenges of X-ray data and how their approach addresses them.

(ii) As pointed out  by Reviewer etwN, the experiments are limited to chest X-ray/CT datasets, which does not fully support the claim of achieving “Explainable Vision–Language Alignment in Radiology.” The title and narrative of the paper must be revised to avoid the generic "radiology" term for  better aligning with the actual scope of experiments and results.

(iii) The authors are also expected to incorporate all additional explanations and experimental results provided in the rebuttal and discussion into the final draft (or supplementary material if space is limited).

(iv)  Moreover, as promised in the NeurIPS submission portal, the authors are expected to open-source the code and training data or provide clear guidance for adapting the publicly available codebases and datasets, to ensure reproducibility of the reported experimental results.
Thanks for providing the additional evidence. My concerns have been fully resolved, and I will maintain my current score.

Continuing from the previous comment, we address the remaining points below.

**Q2: Open-vocabulary capability**

> The model is only validated on chest CT scans, which falls far short of the paper’s assertion of achieving “Explainable Vision–Language Alignment in Radiology.”

Our intention with the phrase “Vision–Language Alignment in Radiology” in the title was to indicate that our work addresses vision-language alignment within the domain of radiology, and chest X-rays are a representative and widely studied modality within this field. We did not mean to imply coverage of all radiological modalities. We apologize if the wording caused any confusion.

That said, our proposed method is not limited to chest X-rays and is designed to be generalizable to other radiology domains, such as chest CT. Extending our approach to additional imaging modalities is a natural direction for future work.

**Q3: Choice of finding-sentences and Comparison to [1]**

Using visual-aspect descriptions, [1] constructed a fixed set of descriptions for 75 predefined medical findings during training, thereby limiting the model training to a fixed finding set.
In contrast, our approach extracts finding-sentences directly from radiology reports, enabling the model to handle an unrestricted and diverse set of findings as they naturally occur in the data, without being limited to a predefined label set.

At inference time, [1] highlights the ability to handle unseen diseases by generating visual-aspect descriptions using an LLM. However, for classes beyond the 75 findings defined in [1], which are considered unseen for their model, our model is still likely to have encountered such expressions during training if they are at all plausible in the context of chest X-ray reports.
To further validate this point, we performed zero-shot classification on the same dataset used in [1], evaluating performance via the area under the ROC curve (AUC).


|**Method**|**PadChest-seen**|**PadChest-unseen**|**PadChest-rare**|**ChestXray-14**|**CheXpert**|
|-|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
|MAVL [1]|0.788|0.704|0.701|0.736|**0.901**|
|**RadZero**|**0.829**|**0.837**|**0.833**|**0.776**|0.894|

On datasets composed of commonly used disease categories such as ChestXray14 and CheXpert, our model performs comparably to MAVL [1], with relative performance varying by dataset.
However, on the PadChest dataset which contains a far more diverse set of disease classes, our model significantly outperforms MAVL. This performance gap is particularly pronounced on rare diseases and even more so on unseen classes, which [1] highlights as a key advantage of their method.

We follow the same unseen class definition as [1], i.e., diseases not among the 75 predefined categories used during training. Naturally, many of these diseases are likely to appear in our training dataset as part of the extracted finding-sentences. While this might raise concerns about a potentially unfair comparison, this phenomenon itself reflects a key strength of our approach: by not restricting the training to a fixed class set, our approach is able to learn from a broader range of findings without explicit class definitions. This flexibility contributes to greater robustness and generalization compared to class-limited methods like [1].

We thank the reviewer for pointing out a highly relevant existing method within this research area, which we had initially overlooked as a comparison target. This suggestion allowed us to conduct a more detailed comparative analysis with prior work. We will incorporate the comparison results into the revised manuscript and include the paper in the reference list.

[1] Phan, Vu Minh Hieu, et al. "Decomposing disease descriptions for enhanced pathology detection." CVPR, 2024.

[2] Ranasinghe, Kanchana, et al. "Perceptual grouping in contrastive vision-language models." ICCV, 2023.

[3] Wu, Size, et al. "Clipself: Vision transformer distills itself for open-vocabulary dense prediction." ICLR, 2024.

[4] Jose, Cijo, et al. "Dinov2 meets text: A unified framework for image-and pixel-level vision-language alignment." CVPR, 2025.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and detailed questions. Below, we provide responses to each of the three questions, along with a comparison to the referenced study [1].

**Q1: Patch-level vision-language similarity**

Our method uses only global image-text pair supervision and a contrastive learning objective to achieve fine-grained alignment, a widely adopted strategy in prior works including CLIPpy [2], CLIPSelf [3], and dino.txt [4].
We train the model to maximize the consine similarity between a global vision embedding $V$ and its paired text embedding $T$, while minimizing similarity for mismatched pairs.

VL-CABS constructs $V$ as a similarity-weighted sum of all patch embeddings $p_i$. 
For the global similarity $\mathrm{sim}(V, T)$ to be high, at least one patch embedding $p_i$ must exhibit high $\mathrm{sim}(p_i, T)$, and conversely, all $\mathrm{sim}(p_i, T)$ must be low for $\mathrm{sim}(V, T)$ to be low. 
Although supervision is provided solely at the global level, this contrastive structure implicitly encourages fine-grained alignment, as the model must assign higher weights to semantically relevant patches to maximize global similarity.
As a result, meaningful patch-text correlations emerge naturally during training, even in the absence of explicit patch-level supervision.

This effect is particularly evident in radiology, where each finding-sentence typically refers to a highly localized region (e.g., “pleural effusion in the right lower lung”).
Even without patch- or mask-level labels, the model learns to assign large weights to those patches that best match each finding-sentence.

If the reviewer’s notion of “truly fine-grained visual–language alignment” refers to explicit patch-level supervision, we acknowledge that our method does not incorporate such supervision.
However, obtaining patch- or mask-level annotations for every finding-sentence is impractical in our setting: our dataset contains approximately 260K unique sentences, spanning arbitrary finding descriptions. Manually labeling a segmentation mask for each of these sentences would be infeasible. The demonstration that VL-CABS can nonetheless learn meaningful patch-text correlations from only image-text pairs represents a significant advance toward open-vocabulary, zero-shot learning across multiple tasks.

**Q2: Open-vocabulary capability**

> The authors have no ground-truth annotations linking image patches to finding sentences, relying solely on image-level alignment.

We believe our response to the first question (Q1) also addresses this concern.

> The amount of training data used is relatively small for a vision–language alignment task

We agree that the amount of training data may be insufficient for training vision–language alignment models from scratch. However, as shown in our rebuttal experiments on the use of pretrained models, our method successfully achieves alignment by leveraging a self-supervised vision encoder trained to capture fine-grained visual features. Even DINOv2, which is trained solely on natural images, showed promising results. By utilizing XrayDINOv2 pretrained on chest X-rays, RadZero demonstrated even better performance, despite being trained on a relatively small dataset.

> I believe it unlikely that such a simple, small-scale training regime can elicit the claimed “open-vocabulary” segmentation capability in medical imaging domain.

Given that our dataset suffices for vision-language alignment, VL-CABS enables open-vocabulary segmentation in the medical domain.
Fine-grained image-text similarity is computed without explicit patch-level supervision, as global contrastive learning implicitly guides the model to attend to semantically relevant patches.
Since the training dataset contains a wide range of vocabulary used in radiology reports, the learned embedding space is semantically rich.
This allows the model to map free-form textual inputs to embeddings that are semantically close, enabling effective image-text similarity computation.
The resulting pixel-level VL similarity map enables segmentation via simple thresholding, thereby supporting open-vocabulary segmentation.

> How does the model establish relationships between unseen classes and seen classes?

Our method may struggle with truly out-of-distribution diseases such as “COVID-19.” However, because our training data spans a broad radiology vocabulary, the learned embedding space is semantically rich. By using finding-sentences that preserve as much of the original report wording as possible, we expand the in-distribution vocabulary coverage and thereby shrink the set of genuinely unseen classes. Compared to prior work [1], this allows us to handle a much wider range of diseases, boosting both robustness and generalizability. We further discuss this in our response to the last question (Q3), supported by additional experiments.

(We address the remaining points in the following comment.)

Thank you for your further clarification. I acknowledge that the proposed method leverages finding-sentences and utilizes pixel-level similarity map for segmentation (essentially simple thresholding). With that said, I remain unconvinced that these enhancements constitute a substantive technical advance over existing methods, given that both techniques are commonly adopted in vision–language alignment and zero-shot learning. Specifically:
1. Questions regarding patch-level vision–language similarity: After computing patch-level vision–language similarities, the authors introduce no supervisory signal to teach the model which image details correspond to which textual elements. Instead, they perform a weighted sum of the vision token sequence based on similarity scores to derive a single global vision embedding. In other words, the visual–language alignment remains at the image level, which does not, in my view, establish truly fine-grained visual–language correlations. 
2. Questions regarding open‐vocabulary capability: The authors have no ground-truth annotations linking image patches to finding sentences, relying solely on image-level alignment. Furthermore, the amount of training data used is relatively small for a vision–language alignment task. I believe it unlikely that such a simple, small-scale training regime can elicit the claimed “open-vocabulary” segmentation capability in medical imaging domain. How does the model establish relationships between unseen classes and seen classes? Moreover, the model is only validated on chest CT scans, which falls far short of the paper’s assertion of achieving “Explainable Vision–Language Alignment in Radiology.”
3. Choice of finding-sentences vs. fine-grained descriptions: Why are finding-sentences—e.g., “There is pleural effusion in the right lower lung”—more advantageous than more detailed visual-aspect descriptions of pathology? The authors have not compared their approach to the method in [1], despite it being one of the most relevant existing techniques in this area.

[1] Phan, Vu Minh Hieu, et al. "Decomposing disease descriptions for enhanced pathology detection." CVPR, 2024.

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the novelty of our approach. We would like to emphasize the following distinctions that set our approach apart from prior works [1,2]:

**1. Fine-grained image-text similarity**

* **Report decomposition vs. fixed label sets.** In [1], each report is mapped to a fixed set of disease classification labels, and each disease is represented by eight predefined visual-aspect descriptions. 
By contrast, we decompose a free-text report into minimal semantic “finding-sentences” (e.g., “There is pleural effusion in the right lower lung”). 
This enables true zero-shot alignment of arbitrary free-text inputs and underlies RadZero’s open-vocabulary semantic segmentation. In [1], only disease-level predictions are possible, and free-text or open-vocabulary inputs cannot be handled.

* **Vision-language similarity vs. Transformer-based attention probability.** 
Prior Transformer decoder-based methods (e.g., MAVL [1], MedKlip [3], CARZero [4]) rely on attention probabilities, which lack a fixed scale and cannot be thresholded for segmentation. VL-CABS instead computes direct patch-level vision-language similarity via cosine similarity between text and patch embeddings.
By enforcing that patch embeddings, text-aware vision embeddings, and text embeddings share a common vector space, VL-CABS produces direct, pixel-level similarity scores that are both explainable and immediately usable for segmentation through simple thresholding.
Please refer to 
Appendix A (Are Attention Maps of Medical VLMs Explainable?) and §5.2 (VL similarity map analysis)
for a detailed explanation of how our approach differs from prior work.

* **No mask supervision required.** Although [2] applies zero-shot lesion segmentation, it still requires lesion-mask annotations for supervision to learn fine-grained vision-language relationships. In contrast, VL-CABS learns fine-grained, pixel-level similarity solely from global image-report pairs: therefore, no mask labels are needed.


**2. Multi-positive contrastive learning**

Below is a detailed comparison of how [2] and our method differ in 
their application of the
multi-positive NCE (MP-NCE) loss [5], organized into three key points:

1. **Embedding generation**

   * **[2]:** Mask embeddings are produced independently of text by applying cross-attention between learned mask tokens and image features. The same mask embedding is then paired with each of its lesion’s attribute descriptions.
   * **Ours:** We compute cosine similarity directly between text embeddings (of finding-sentences) and patch embeddings to form text-aware vision embeddings. Each positive pair uses this joint text-vision embedding, tightly coupling text and image representations.

2. **Definition of positive pairs**

   * **[2]:** For each lesion, there are eight predefined attribute descriptions, and all eight serve as positive text examples for a single mask embedding.
   * **Ours:** We decompose the full radiology report into minimal “finding-sentences”, and each finding-sentence is treated as its own positive example for the corresponding image. This lets us leverage the full report-image relationship rather than lesion-attribute pairs.

3. **Negative-pair sampling**

   * **[2]:** Negative examples come from attribute descriptions of other lesions within the *same image*, exploiting intra-image diversity.
   * **Ours:** We sample negatives from the paired finding-sentences of *other images* in the batch, leveraging inter-image variation to encourage more discriminative, global alignment.

In summary, by decomposing free-text reports into minimal finding-sentences and aligning them with local image regions via VL-CABS, in which text and patch embeddings share a common space, our method achieves truly fine-grained image-text similarity learning using only global image-text pair supervision.
Building on this, we adopt the MP-NCE loss [5] in a way that uniquely leverages the structure of full radiology reports: each decomposed sentence serves as a distinct, semantically meaningful positive pair for contrastive learning. This unified framework allows the model to learn interpretable, pixel-level alignment solely from image-report pairs, without the need for any structured annotations.

[1] Phan, Vu Minh Hieu, et al. "Decomposing disease descriptions for enhanced pathology detection." CVPR, 2024.

[2] Jiang, Yankai, et al. "Unleashing the Potential of Vision-Language Pre-Training for 3D Zero-Shot Lesion Segmentation." ICLR, 2025.

[3] Wu, Chaoyi, et al. "Medklip: Medical knowledge enhanced language-image pre-training for x-ray diagnosis." ICCV, 2023

[4] Lai, Haoran, et al. "Carzero: Cross-attention alignment for radiology zero-shot classification." CVPR, 2024.

[5] Lee, Janghyeon, et al. "Uniclip: Unified framework for contrastive language-image pre-training." NeurIPS, 2022.

We appreciate the constructive and incisive feedback. We hope our responses address the reviewer's concerns.

> Concerns over reliance on pretrained models (e.g., limited adaptability or bias), with suggestions of self-supervised learning or fine-tuning

We thank the reviewer for highlighting the dependency on pretrained models. Our approach currently uses a domain-specific vision encoder (XrayDINOv2) pretrained on X-ray images. To assess this dependency, we conducted experiments with three vision encoder settings: (1) ViT trained from scratch, (2) frozen DINOv2 pretrained on natural images, and (3) frozen XrayDINOv2. This setup evaluates both the necessity of pretraining and the role of domain specificity.

|Vision encoder|OI|PC|PC20|CXR14|CXP|CXD10|Grnd|Phr-Grnd|SIIM (AUC)|SIIM (Dice)|RSNA (AUC)|RSNA (Dice)|
|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
ViT from scratch|0.700|0.728|0.693|0.704|0.848|0.643|0.237|0.611|0.773|0.023|0.751|0.379|
DINOv2|0.841|0.825|0.853|0.791|**0.901**|**0.794**|0.606|0.814|0.908|0.100|**0.856**|0.509|
**XrayDINOv2 (RadZero)**|**0.847**|**0.841**|**0.871**|**0.804**|0.900|0.787|**0.622**|**0.844**|**0.924**|**0.171**|0.834|**0.546**|

*Grnd* and *Phr-Grnd* refer to grounding and phrase grounding, respectively.

Training from scratch led to substantial degradation across all metrics, confirming some dependency on pretrained weights for effective learning.
However, domain-specific pretraining is not strictly required: the model with DINOv2 (pretrained on natural images) achieved competitive results and even outperformed RadZero on some metrics. This shows that general-domain models can be effectively adapted to the X-ray domain.
Furthermore, it suggests that our method can be applied to domains lacking domain-specific pretrained vision encoders, broadening its applicability while mitigating the risk of domain-specific biases.

A similar observation holds for the language encoder. Although MPNet, the language model used in our study, was not pretrained on medical texts, 
it successfully learned vision-language alignment using X-ray image–report pairs. This further supports the adaptability of our method across domains without domain-specific language pretraining.

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable suggestions on self-supervised learning and fine-tuning. We agree that self-supervised learning is a promising direction and plan to explore it in future work. For fine-tuning, we assessed its impact on both computational efficiency and performance. 
Due to increased computational overhead, memory usage rises and maintaining the same batch size becomes infeasible. Training time also increases. The table below compares memory and training time for freezing vs. fine-tuning the vision encoder under the same setup (batch size 64 on 4×H100 GPUs).

|Vision encoder|Training GPU memory↓ (GB)|Training GPU hour↓|
|-|-|-|
|Freeze|18.52 x 4|56|
|Unfreeze|51.70 x 4|100|

Fine-tuning requires approximately three times more memory and nearly twice the training time compared to freezing the vision encoder.

|Vision encoder|OI|PC|PC20|CXR14|CXP|CXD10|Grnd|Phr-Grnd|SIIM (AUC)|SIIM (Dice)|RSNA (AUC)|RSNA (Dice)|
|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
**Freeze(RadZero)**|0.847|**0.841**|**0.871**|0.804|0.900|**0.787**|**0.622**|**0.844**|0.924|**0.171**|0.834|**0.546**|
Unfreeze|**0.852**|0.800|0.777|**0.818**|**0.903**|0.779|0.400|0.760|**0.932**|0.113|**0.848**|0.496|

Fine-tuning the vision encoder yielded only marginal classification gains over RadZero on some datasets, while performance on fine-grained tasks dropped notably. In particular, the fine-tuned model performed significantly worse on PadChest20, which contains rare classes—suggesting reduced generalization. This aligns with [1], which reports that freezing the vision encoder can enhance generalizability. Given the high computational cost of fine-tuning, limited classification improvements, significant fine-grained degradation, and reduced generalization, we conclude that freezing the vision encoder is a more efficient and effective choice for our setting.

> Multi-positive contrastive learning risks overfitting to specific report formats.

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding potential overfitting. In our case, this risk is mitigated by the diverse linguistic and syntactic patterns introduced through LLM-based extraction of “finding sentences” during training. To validate robustness, we built a vector database of training sentences using RadZero’s text encoder and conducted similarity searches. For example, given the query "the lungs are clear," the model retrieved varied semantically similar sentences, showing no overfitting to fixed templates. (Similarity scores in parentheses.)
```
Query: the lungs are clear
1.The lungs are clear (1.000)
2.Lungs are clear (0.994)
3.The airways are clear (0.993)
4.There is clear lungs (0.985)
5.There are clear lungs (0.983)
6.The chest is clear (0.982)
```
Despite not following the "[There is ...]" pattern, the model retrieved semantically similar sentences such as "chest is clear" and "airways are clear", confirming that the encoder is not restricted to a fixed sentence structure.

We also tested syntactic diversity with "pleural effusion in the right lower lung": 
```
Query: pleural effusion in the right lower lung
1.There is pleural effusion in the right lower lung (0.993)
...
5.There is a pleural effusion of the right lower lung (0.965)
6.There is right lower lung pleural effusion (0.953)
```
The model returned variants like "right lower lung pleural effusion" and "pleural effusion of the right lower lung": it captured the underlying semantics across different grammatical constructions.

To test lexical flexibility, we queried "there is fibrosis":
```
Query: there is fibrosis
1.There is fibrosis (1.000)
2.There is probable fibrosis (0.937)
3.There is lung fibrosis (0.937)
4.There is chronic fibrosis (0.934)
5.There is a component of fibrosis (0.924)
6.There is fibrotic disease (0.917)
```
The retrieved sentences included "chronic fibrosis" and "fibrotic disease", indicating the model understands semantics beyond the exact query vocabulary.

These results suggest that our model is not restricted to specific templates or vocabularies and generalizes well across linguistic variations, reducing the risk of overfitting.

However, we acknowledge that the model may not generate well-aligned embeddings for report expressions that were rare or absent in the training data. 
One known case is abbreviations—for example, the abbreviation “RLL” (right lower lung) was rarely used in the original reports. As a result, embeddings for abbreviations may be less accurate or semantically weaker compared to those of their expanded counterparts.

```
Edge case: pleural effusion in RLL (unseen format)
1.There is pleural effusion with drainage (0.753)
2.There is slight decrease in pleural fluid (0.725)
3.There is collecting pleural fluid (0.708)
```
To address this issue, non-standardized inputs—such as free-form reports with abbreviations or unusual phrasing—can be rewritten into finding-sentences using an LLM. This helps prevent performance degradation and ensures robust generalization across diverse report styles.

Even so, we believe that such overfitting is unlikely to be directly caused by the multi-positive contrastive learning framework. We are concerned that we may have misunderstood the reviewer’s point, and if the reviewer meant a different aspect of overfitting, we would greatly appreciate further clarification.

> VL-CABS similarity maps enhance interpretability, but are they clinically useful?

We agree with the reviewer that improved interpretability does not necessarily guarantee clinical utility. We also found this to be an important question and conducted a reader study with clinically trained readers to assess whether the model’s outputs improve readers' understanding of radiographic findings. The evaluation results indicate that our model has the potential to support clinical interpretation, and we are currently preparing a separate clinical paper based on these findings. Due to IRB constraints, we are unable to include detailed outcomes in this discussion, but we sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s understanding as we prepare the manuscript for publication.

> Efficiency–cost trade-offs for high-resolution inputs, along with suggestions of model compression

As the reviewer correctly pointed out, increasing image resolution leads to higher computational cost. To quantify this trade-off, we compared 224px and 518px models in terms of performance and resource usage. The table below summarizes the results:

|Resolution|Training GPU Memory↓ (GB)|Training GPU hour↓|Inference GPU Memory↓ (GB)|Latency↓ (ms/img)|Throughput (img/s)|Cls (AUC)|Grnd (ACC)|Seg (DICE)|
|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
|224px|25.13 x 4|40|2.20|60.18|733.56|0.852|0.537|0.342|
|518px|73.36 x 4|52|2.38|70.05|94.93|0.851|0.622|0.359|

The reported performance in the table reflects the average across all datasets for each task. These results suggest that the added computational cost is a worthwhile trade-off considering the significant gains in fine-grained performance.

As suggested by the reviewer, we conducted a model compression experiment via pruning. Specifically, we applied 10% L1-norm-based structured pruning to the MLP layers of the vision encoder.

|Method|Num. of Parameters|Throughput (img/s)|Cls (AUC)|
|-|-|-|-|
|**RadZero**|209M|94.93|0.851|
|Pruning10%|203M|97.16|0.680|

Pruning reduced the vision encoder’s parameters from 85.7M to 80.1M and the total model size from 209M to 204M, yielding a modest 2.3% gain in inference speed but noticeable performance degradation. While fine-tuning may recover accuracy, the trade-off may not justify the added cost. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and believe model compression for efficiency remains a promising direction.

[1] Zhai, Xiaohua, et al. "Lit: Zero-shot transfer with locked-image text tuning." CVPR, 2022.

Freezing the vision encoder allows us to preserve fine-grained visual features, while the vision-language alignment enables a language interface through the text encoder—effectively bridging the strengths of self-supervised vision models and VLM approaches.

summary.value: The paper presents RadZero, a novel vision-language alignment model for radiology, featuring VL-CABS, a similarity-based cross-attention mechanism that aligns text embeddings with local image features for interpretable, fine-grained reasoning. Using large language models, RadZero extracts concise semantic sentences from radiology reports and employs multi-positive contrastive learning to align images with multiple textual descriptions, enabling robust representation learning without pixel-level annotations. With a pre-trained vision encoder and trainable Transformer layers, it efficiently handles high-resolution chest radiographs. RadZero achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot classification, grounding, and segmentation on public benchmarks, with VL similarity maps enhancing explainability and supporting open-vocabulary semantic segmentation.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strength**：

1、Enhanced Interpretability: RadZero's VL-CABS mechanism generates pixel-level similarity maps by computing cosine similarity between text and image features, offering transparent and fine-grained visual reasoning that significantly improves clinical interpretability compared to traditional attention maps.

**Weaknesses**：

1、Dependence on Pre-trained Models: RadZero relies on pre-trained vision (e.g., XrayDINOv2) and language models, which may limit adaptability to new data distributions and introduce biases from pre-training data.
2、Limited Generalization: Despite strong performance on public chest radiograph benchmarks, RadZero underperforms on certain datasets, indicating constrained generalization to diverse or uncommon cases.
3、Risk of Overfitting: Multi-positive contrastive learning may lead to overfitting to specific report formats or vocabularies if training data lacks diversity, potentially reducing performance on varied report structures.

questions.value:
1、 The model’s reliance on pretrained vision and language models may limit adaptability and introduce biases. Can this dependency be reduced? Consider self-supervised learning or partial fine-tuning and compare performance (e.g., accuracy) with and without pretrained weights.

3、 VL-CABS similarity maps enhance interpretability, but are they clinically useful? I suggest a small clinician user study to validate their impact on diagnosis (e.g., diagnostic accuracy). 

4、High-resolution image processing increases computational cost. How can efficiency be optimized? Explore model compression (e.g., pruning) and report performance (e.g., accuracy) versus resource use (e.g., inference time).

summary.value:
The paper introduces **RadZero**, a vision–language (VL) pre-training framework for chest-radiograph interpretation that targets *zero-shot* classification, grounding, segmentation, and open-vocabulary semantic segmentation.

Key novelties are:

- **VL-CABS (Vision-Language Cross-Attention Based on Similarity):** a patch-level cross-attention mechanism that replaces the usual dot-product with *scaled cosine similarity*, producing well-calibrated similarity maps that double as both logits and interpretable heat-maps.
- **Multi-positive contrastive training:** every image is paired with *all* “finding-sentences” extracted from its report with an LLM, and the Multi-Positive NCE loss is used to aggregate supervision without random sampling.
- **High-resolution but lightweight vision backbone:** a frozen XrayDINOv2 encoder is fed 518 px images, while only two extra transformer layers are trained, yielding high spatial fidelity at modest cost.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
## Strengths

Large-scale ablation isolates the effect of similarity metric, trainable layers, multi-positive loss and resolution; results are consistent across 0-shot tasks. 

Combines ideas (LiT freezing, dino.txt layers, MP-NCE) into a cohesive medical VLM.

VL-CABS’ use of cosine similarity as both logit and heat-map is neat and, to my knowledge, novel.

## weakness

High-resolution inputs (518 px) improve grounding and segmentation but at a memory/latency cost, and they sometimes degrade classification. The paper lacks a systematic analysis of this trade-off or guidance on when the extra cost is warranted.

RadZero freezes XrayDINOv2 trained at 224 px, then feeds 518 px images.  This mismatch slightly hurts classification accuracy and is acknowledged.

questions.value:
1. **Similarity notation** – consider defining the scaled cosine similarity once as
    
    $s_{imk}^{n} = \frac{\langle v_{ik},t_j^{n}\rangle}{\tau}$
    
2. **Compute cost vs. benefit** – Given that higher resolution (518 px) helps grounding but slightly hurts classification (Table 5), would a *mixed-resolution* strategy (224 px in early epochs, 518 px for finetuning) recover both?

3. **Statistical significance** – Please report per-task standard errors or run-seed variance so reviewers can judge whether gains (e.g., =- 0.014 AUC on OI) are robust.

limitations.value: The authors provide a frank discussion (Sec 6) of generalisation gaps and reliance on a frozen 224-px pre-trained encoder. I agree with this assessment and appreciate the transparency. Yes, limitations and societal impacts are adequately addressed.

I especially appreciate the effort involved in running new experiments to address my questions: Compute/Performance Trade-off and Statistical Significance. While the authors have been transparent about this limitation and have answered my questions, the underlying technical challenge of using a frozen encoder with a different resolution than it was trained on remains an inherent, unsolved weakness of the proposed method.

summary.value: This paper presents RadZero, a vision-language alignment model for radiology that supports zero-shot classification, grounding, and segmentation. It introduces VL-CABS, which uses cosine similarity between text and image patches to produce interpretable similarity maps. The model employs a frozen vision encoder, lightweight Transformer layers, and trains with multi-positive contrastive learning to align each image with multiple report sentences. Experiments on public chest X-ray datasets demonstrate strong performance and improved explainability.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

1.  The paper extends contrastive learning to align each image with multiple semantically minimal sentences extracted from radiology reports. This multi-positive formulation improves training stability and semantic diversity, which is especially valuable in clinical vision-language tasks with complex text-image relationships.

2. The evaluation includes nearly all major public chest X-ray datasets, covering a wide range of zero-shot tasks (classification, grounding, segmentation, phrase grounding). This makes the claims empirically convincing and the conclusions broadly applicable within the medical vision-language domain.

3. Beyond technical design, the paper demonstrates high quality in writing, reproducibility, and transparency. The authors provide implementation details, ablations, and commit to open-sourcing code and models, which reflects strong community contribution standards.

Weaknesses:

1. The optimization objective remains at the global image-text level; although patch similarities are computed, they are only used for pooling and visualization, not directly supervised. As a result, VL-CABS does not explicitly optimize patch-level alignment.

2. Despite strong design and wide evaluation, the model does not clearly outperform prior methods (e.g., CARZero or MedKLIP) across all tasks and datasets. In particular, its gains in classification are modest, and grounding/segmentation improvements rely partly on higher resolution inputs.

3. While the VL similarity map is a central contribution of the paper, it is never explicitly supervised or optimized. It is only derived post-hoc from global alignment signals, raising concerns about whether it can be reliably used for pixel-level reasoning or segmentation beyond visualization.

4. Many of RadZero’s reported improvements in grounding and segmentation rely on high-resolution inputs (518px), while competing methods are evaluated at 224px. Ablation shows significant performance drop at lower resolution, suggesting that part of the gain may come from resolution scaling rather than architectural advances.

questions.value:
1. VL similarity maps are central to your interpretability claims but are not directly supervised during training. Have you considered adding auxiliary losses (e.g., from pseudo labels or phrase-region alignments) to explicitly optimize these maps? If so, what were the results?

2. In Table 1, RadZero underperforms CARZero on CXR14 and CheXpert in zero-shot classification. Could you elaborate on why your model may be less effective on these task-driven benchmarks? Is there a trade-off between RadZero's grounding-focused architecture and global classification performance?

3. You chose to freeze the vision encoder throughout training. Could you clarify the motivation behind this decision? Have you considered finetuning it to further improve alignment quality or performance on classification tasks?

limitations.value:
1. VL similarity maps are not directly supervised, which raises concerns about their reliability for fine-grained grounding or segmentation beyond visualization. Adding auxiliary losses or weak supervision could improve alignment quality.

2. The reported improvements in grounding and segmentation rely heavily on higher input resolution (518px), while most baselines use 224px. The potential confounding effect of resolution is not fully controlled or discussed.

3. While the method is positioned as interpretable, the similarity maps are only weakly correlated with clinical annotations, and no radiologist or human validation is reported to confirm interpretability or safety in deployment contexts.

summary.value: The authors present a framework - RadZero - for vision-language alignment in radiology, focusing on chest x-rays. The framework encompasses several zero-shot downstream tasks, including classification, grounding, and segmentation. The approach is evaluated using several public datasets, achieving promising results.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. The manuscript is well written and generally easy to follow. 
2. The approach is intuitive and the motivation compared to prior works is logical.
3. Extensive evaluation is performed across many datasets and tasks, including ablation analyses.
4. The zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation results are intriguing, where the model is reasonably able to segment different anatomical regions in addition to performing pathology classification.

Weaknesses
1. The paper could further be improved by additional comparison to supervised baselines. Such benchmarking is reported for the segmentation results, but not for classification. Reporting such results (for at least a subset of the datasets) would help provide additional context on the level of performance.
2. While the performance for grounding and segmentation is meaningfully higher than the prior CARZero model, the improvement in classification is less dramatic, with underperformance on some datasets.
3. As is typical in contrastive learning settings, text phrases from the same image are treated as positive pairs and other images are treated as negatives. However, in the current approach where the text phrase is first standardized to a simplified "finding-sentence", for instance "There is no pneumothorax", this simple negative/positive assignment seems suboptimal. For instance, a similar finding-sentence may also be present for another image in the training batch, where it seems like this could be automatically determined and be treated instead as a positive example.
4. In the paper checklist, the authors check "No" for the inclusion of error bars b/c "it would be too computationally expensive". Error bars could be computed via bootstrapping of the predictions, which is not computationally expensive. 
5. Subgroup performance by pathology is reported for zero-shot grounding but not classification. This would also be helpful to see for classification.

Other clarifications/minor comments:
1. In Figure 3, is the Text Encoder also frozen or just the Vision Encoder?
2. The difference between "grounding" and "phrase grounding" is not entirely clear.
3. In line 88, "G2D [21]" appears twice.
4. Line 198: "Following [36], we compute the Dice score using only positive samples and optimize the segmentation threshold to maximize the score." - Is this optimization performed on the test data itself? Is it done separately per dataset?

questions.value:
Suggestions that would improve my enthusiasm:
1. Inclusion of supervised baseline for classification.
2. Inclusion of error bars.
3. Reporting of subgroup performance by pathology for classification. 

Clarifications:
1. Further details on how the segmentation threshold is chosen
2. Difference between "grounding" and "phrase grounding"

final_justification.value: I thank the authors for their clarifications and additional experiments included. I have upgraded by score to 6: Strong Accept due to the added experiments regarding baselines, error bars, and subgroup performance. I do have a remaining concern that the segmentation threshold was chosen based on the test set, as this likely causes overfitting and it should instead be chosen on the validation split. I recommend that the authors make this fix in the final version, but I believe that the volume of other experiments and contributions still warrant a Strong Accept.

title.value: RadZero: Similarity-Based Cross-Attention for Explainable Vision-Language Alignment in Chest X-ray with Zero-Shot Multi-Task Capability

abstract.value:
Recent advancements in multimodal models have significantly improved vision-language (VL) alignment in radiology. 
However, existing approaches struggle to effectively utilize complex radiology reports for learning and offer limited interpretability through attention probability visualizations.
To address these challenges, we introduce $\textbf{RadZero}$, a novel framework for VL alignment in chest X-ray with zero-shot multi-task capability.
A key component of our approach is $\textbf{VL-CABS}$ ($\textbf{V}$ision-$\textbf{L}$anguage $\textbf{C}$ross-$\textbf{A}$ttention $\textbf{B}$ased on $\textbf{S}$imilarity), which aligns text embeddings with local image features for interpretable, fine-grained VL reasoning.
RadZero leverages large language models to extract concise semantic sentences from radiology reports and employs multi-positive contrastive training to effectively capture relationships between images and multiple relevant textual descriptions. 
It uses a pre-trained vision encoder with additional trainable Transformer layers, allowing efficient high-resolution image processing. 
By computing similarity between text embeddings and local image patch features, VL-CABS enables zero-shot inference with similarity 
probability for classification, and pixel-level VL similarity maps for grounding and segmentation. 
Experimental results on public chest radiograph benchmarks show that RadZero outperforms state-of-the-art methods in zero-shot classification, grounding, and segmentation. 
Furthermore, VL similarity map analysis highlights the potential of VL-CABS for improving explainability in VL alignment. 
Additionally, qualitative evaluation demonstrates RadZero's capability for open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, further validating its effectiveness in medical imaging.
Code is available at https://github.com/deepnoid-ai/RadZero.
